inline.s: Course
Textbook

The Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching Sutra is the Buddha's final instruction to his disciples before entering nirvāṇa, in which he specially and concisely urged them again on how to cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom, so as to escape afflictions and birth and death.
Master Ouyi said:
“When Xi
(Master Ouyi's self-reference; the Master's name was Zhi Xi)
had not yet left home, upon reading this Final Teaching, he knew that every word was blood and tears; and after receiving the shaving and dyeing, he did not dare to forget it even slightly
(not daring to forget it in the least)
.” “To follow it and practice it is to be a Dharma-son; not to follow this instruction is to be one who rebels and is unfilial.”

(The Explanation of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching Sutra). We children of the Buddha should surely recite it often and practice it often, so as to perfect the career of the Way and repay the Buddha's profound kindness.
[Shaving and dyeing] Shaving off the beard and hair, wearing the dyed robe, and leaving home to become a monk.
Note: For ease of understanding and reference, each passage is preceded by a number and a title, none of which belong to the sutra text.

blocks.text: Title of the Sutra and Its Translator

inline.s: [The Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching Sutra]

Bequeathed teaching” means the instruction given at the moment of death. “The Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching Sutra” is an abbreviated name for “The Sutra Wherein the Buddha, Being About to Enter Nirvāṇa, Briefly Speaks the Teaching of Instruction” - the words of the World-Honored One's final instruction to his disciples, concisely and pointedly teaching how to cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom, so as to escape afflictions and birth and death.
Master Ouyi, in his Explanation of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching Sutra, says:

“‘Bequeath’ means to leave behind; ‘teaching’ means instruction. It is like what the Confucian books call the ‘charge at the time of death’, and what in the world of mortals is called a will. To follow it and practice it is to be a Dharma-son; not to follow this instruction is to be one who rebels and is unfilial.”

[Bequeath (yí) to leave behind] Hand down. [Confucian books] Confucian writings. [Charge at the time of death] The last edict of an emperor. [Dharma-son] Whoever follows the Buddha's Way and is nourished by the Dharma is called a Dharma-son. Here “Dharma-son” means a son of the Dharma King (the Buddha).
[Also called “The Sutra Wherein the Buddha, Being About to Enter Nirvāṇa, Briefly Speaks the Teaching of Instruction”]

It is also called “The Sutra Wherein the Buddha, Being About to Enter Nirvāṇa, Briefly Speaks the Teaching of Instruction”; this is the concise and clear instruction given by the Buddha just as he was about to enter nirvāṇa.

[Being about to (chuí)] At the time of entering but not yet entered. [Nirvāṇa] Rendered in Chinese as “yuan ji” (perfect stillness): “yuan” is the perfection of all wisdom and virtue, and “ji” is the stilling of all confusion and karma. It is also translated as “mie du” (extinction and crossing over): “mie” is the extinguishing of the three confusions - the confusions of views and thought, of dust-and-sand, and of ignorance - and “du” is the crossing over of both shared (sectional) birth-and-death and transformative birth-and-death. In short, when a person's wisdom and virtue have both reached the final perfection, and even birth-and-death and afflictions have been transcended, that is called “nirvāṇa.” This is the true-suchness realm, beyond arising and ceasing and beyond time and space, realized by the sages; and it is also the most ideal and most beautiful destination for all the multitudes of beings. [Confusion of views and thought] The confusions of views and of thought. The confusion of views is the deluded error of ordinary people in their views, namely the five wrong views: the view of a self, the view of extremes, the view of denial, the view of clinging to views, and the view of clinging to precepts and prohibitions; the confusion of thought is the deluded error of ordinary people in their thinking, namely the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two confusions are the root of sentient beings’ drifting through the three realms and vainly undergoing birth-and-death; eradicating them, one can end birth-and-death and leave the three realms. [Confusion of dust and sand] This is the confusion of the bodhisattvas. If bodhisattvas, in transforming sentient beings, do not penetrate the countless methods as numerous as dust and sand, they cannot complete the work of teaching and transforming sentient beings; hence it is called the confusion of dust and sand. [Confusion of ignorance] This is fundamental ignorance, which can veil the principle of the real mark of the Middle Way; when it is entirely eradicated, one attains Buddhahood. [Sectional birth-and-death] All sentient beings, in the three realms and six paths, because of the karma of good and evil they have produced, have a limited life-span and a segmented form; hence their birth-and-death is called “sectional birth-and-death.” [Transformative birth-and-death] The sages of the three vehicles (the voice-hearer vehicle, the conditioned-realizer vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle) have already cut off the confusions of views and thought and ended sectional birth-and-death; but because of the result of their way-cultivation, deluded thoughts gradually vanish while realized wisdom gradually increases. This transition of delusion and realization is different in each period; moving from an earlier period to a later one is exactly like a birth-and-death, and its change is wondrous, unfathomable, and inconceivable; hence it is called “transformative birth-and-death” or “inconceivable transformative birth-and-death.” [Briefly speak] Master Ouyi, in his Explanation of the Buddha's Bequeathed Teaching Sutra, says: “When one is about to enter nirvāṇa, there is no further meeting; when it is already the middle of the night, there is not much time left. Therefore the essential points are taken up and briefly spoken, to serve as a final warning. Truly it is no less than one word being one drop of blood! How can the reader not reflect on this?” [Taking up the essential points and briefly speaking] Selecting what is most important and speaking of it concisely. [No less than (
chì
)] None other than.
[Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin]
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumārajīva in the Yao Qin period.

Yao Qin”: in history there have been three Qin dynasties. One is the Qin state of the Warring States period, up to the Qin dynasty in which Qin Shi Huang unified the world; the second Qin dynasty was during the period of the Five Barbarians and Sixteen Kingdoms, whose ruler was Fu Jian; the third Qin dynasty was established when Fu Jian's general Yao Chang killed Fu Jian and set himself up, with the dynastic name also called Qin. Later people, to distinguish it from the Qin dynasty of Fu Jian's time, called it the Yao Qin, also known as the Later Qin.

Tripitaka” means the pitaka of sutras, the pitaka of vinaya, and the pitaka of commentaries. The pitaka of sutras is the scriptures spoken by the Buddha; the pitaka of vinaya is the precepts established by the Buddha; and the pitaka of commentaries is the treatises composed by the Buddha's disciples. A “Tripitaka Master” is a bhikṣu who is thoroughly versed in all three pitakas of sutras, vinaya, and commentaries.
Kumārajīva (

) was originally an Indian, but grew up in Kucha (between present-day Kuqa County and Shaya County in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region). After leaving home, he was well-versed in the Mahāyāna sutras and commentaries. In the third year of the Hongshi era of Yao Xing of the Later Qin (

), he came to Chang'an in China and translated scriptures in the Xiaoyao Garden; the sutras and commentaries he translated in all amounted to more than 380 volumes. In the fifteenth year of the Hongshi era of the Later Qin (

), he passed away in Chang'an. At death he gathered the assembly and took leave, saying: “Meeting because of the Dharma, yet I have not fully exhausted my heart. When I again face the later world, it is a thing of profound sorrow. Considering my own darkness and shortcoming, I was wrongly made to fill the role of translator. Of the sutras and commentaries I produced, only the Ten Recitation Vinaya has not yet been trimmed of its verbosity. If the meaning accords with the Buddha's mind, then on the day my body is burned, my tongue will not be scorched or destroyed.” Having spoken, he passed away. After his death he was cremated, and his tongue, like a red lotus, was not destroyed, proving that the scriptures he translated are absolutely reliable and error-free.

blocks.text: 1. The Origin of the Dharma Assembly

inline.s: [Śākyamuni Buddha, having first turned the wheel of the Dharma, saved Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya. In his final teaching he saved Subhadra. Those who should be saved have all been saved. Between the twin sāla trees, he was about to enter nirvāṇa. At that time, in the middle of the night, all was silent and without sound. For the sake of the disciples, he briefly spoke the essentials of the Dharma.]

Śākyamuni Buddha, having first turned the wheel of the Dharma, saved Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya and the other five. In his final teaching he saved Subhadra. Those who were to be saved have all been saved. Between the twin sāla trees, he was about to enter nirvāṇa. At this time it was the middle of the night, and all around was silent and without sound. For the sake of his disciples, the Buddha briefly spoke the essentials of the Dharma.

Master Ouyi said: “When one is about to enter nirvāṇa, there is no further meeting; when it is already the middle of the night, there is not much time left. Therefore the essential points are taken up and briefly spoken, to serve as a final warning. Truly it is no less than one word being one drop of blood! How can the reader not reflect on this?”

First turning the wheel of the Dharma, saving Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya; in his final teaching, saving Subhadra.” After the Buddha attained the Way, he spoke the Dharma for forty-nine years and saved countless beings. Here he cites the first and the last so as to summarize from beginning to end. Having first turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths in the Deer Park and saved Kauṇḍinya and the other four, then, as he was about to enter nirvāṇa, he saved Subhadra.

[Turning the wheel of the Dharma] The “wheel of the Dharma” is a metaphor for the teaching spoken by the Buddha, which can crush all the afflictions of sentient beings, just as a great wheel can crush all rocks and gravel; and it is also conveyed from person to person, like the turning of a wheel, reaching everywhere without limit. Therefore, the Buddha's expounding the scriptures and teaching the Dharma to save sentient beings is called “turning the wheel of the Dharma.” [Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya] Ājñāta is the given name; Kauṇḍinya is the surname. [Subhadra] Subhadra was the last disciple to receive instruction and attain the Way before the Buddha entered nirvāṇa. When he attained the Way he was already one hundred twenty years old, intelligent and full of wisdom; upon hearing the Buddha speak of the Noble Eightfold Path, he left home and received the precepts that very night, purely cultivating the holy life, and before long in the night he became an arhat, and before the Buddha he first took up his own final nirvāṇa. [Sāla tree] A tall evergreen belonging to the family of the dipterocarpaceae; the trunk can be tapped for camphor (borneol). Camphor is a fine and very precious natural fragrance. Devout disciples of the Buddha often use camphor oil to light the lamps before the Buddha, and often use the heartwood of the sāla tree to burn incense before the Buddha, filling the Buddha hall with a clean fragrance. In India, Thailand, and other countries, after a person dies the body is burned with wood; the rich and the noble often use the sāla tree as fuel. [Twin sāla trees] According to the records of the scriptures, when Śākyamuni Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa outside the city of Kuśinagara, at each of the four sides of his couch there was a pair of sāla trees growing from the same root. Of each pair on each side, one tree, from grief, turned a ghastly white, and its branches, leaves, flowers, fruit, bark, and trunk all burst open, fell away, and gradually withered; the other tree remained. Hence this pair of trees is also called the four-withered four-flourishing trees, or the not-withered not-flourishing trees. For this reason there arise the metaphors of the eastern pair being “eternal and non-eternal,” the western pair “self and non-self,” the southern pair “joy and no-joy,” and the northern pair “pure and impure.” [Middle of the night] In ancient India, time was measured by dividing a day and night into six periods: three daytime periods and three nighttime periods. The three daytime periods are the morning, midday, and sunset; the three nighttime periods are the early night, the middle of the night, and the late night. Thus one period of the “six periods” equals four hours in modern terms, and the six periods equal the modern twenty-four hours. The middle of the night corresponds roughly to ten at night until two in the morning.

[You bhikṣus, after my extinction, should honor, treasure, and revere the Prātimokṣa. It is like meeting light in darkness, or a poor person obtaining a treasure. You should know that this is your great teacher; if I dwelt in the world, it would be no different from this.]

You bhikṣus, after I have entered extinction, should honor, treasure, and revere the Prātimokṣa (the precepts). This is like meeting light in darkness, or a poor person obtaining a treasure. You should know that this is your great teacher, just as if I were in the world personally teaching you.

Master Ouyi said: “When the Buddha was in the world, one took the Buddha as teacher; after the Buddha has passed into extinction, one takes the precepts as teacher. If one cannot uphold the precepts, then even in the same hall one is still separated by ten thousand miles; if one can uphold the precepts, then how is a hundred generations different from the same time? The golden mouth speaks the sincere words thus; how then can one abandon this and seek elsewhere!”

[Bhikṣu] A general term for one who has left home and received the full precepts; the male is called “bhikṣu” and the female “bhikṣuṇī.” [Prātimokṣa] Rendered in meaning as “conformable liberation,” “liberation in every place,” and “specific liberation,” meaning: every time one upholds a precept, one has already planted the cause for a portion of liberation and already gains liberation from the afflictions of the present moment; if one does not uphold the precepts, one is bound by afflictions. If one can be mindful at every moment and uphold the precepts in every place, then one is liberated at every moment and in every place. “Prātimokṣa” is the discipline to be observed by those who have left home; it is the most important core regulation among the subjects of study, and all members of the order should observe it. In later times the content of the Prātimokṣa was collected together to form the Prātimokṣa Sutra, also called the Precepts Sutra, which is the core of the Vinaya Pitaka.

blocks.text: 3. The Marks of Upholding the Precepts

inline.s: [One who upholds the pure precepts must not engage in buying and selling or trade, must not manage fields and houses, must not keep people, slaves, or animals, and must be far from all kinds of planting and all treasures, as if avoiding a pit of fire. He must not cut down trees or grass, must not break the ground or dig the earth, must not prepare medicinal decoctions, must not divine fortune by physiognomy, must not gaze up at the stars, must not calculate the waxing and waning [of the moon], and must not make computations and reckonings - none of these are to be done. He should restrain his body, eat at the proper time, and live purely and cleanly. He must not take part in worldly affairs, must not carry messages or missions, must not practice spells or make elixirs, must not befriend and flatter the powerful and noble, must not associate intimately or rudely. He should rectify his own mind and, with right mindfulness, seek liberation. He must not conceal his own flaws, must not display strange powers to confuse the people, and with respect to the four offerings he should know their measure and be content, only obtaining what is needed for support, and should not store up [goods]. This is a brief statement of the marks of upholding the precepts.]
In teaching the marks of upholding the precepts, the Buddha spoke of four “must nots”:

First, one who upholds the pure precepts must not do business or trade, must not manage fields and houses, must not keep people (those who are not in the position of slaves) or slaves and animals, and must not plant crops or store up treasures; all of these should be kept far away, as if avoiding a pit of fire.

Second, one who upholds the pure precepts must not cut down flowers, plants, and trees, must not break the soil or dig the earth, and must not prepare medicinal decoctions for others, divine fortunes, read physiognomy, observe the stars for prognostication, or compute the calendar; none of the above should be done. One should be diligent and frugal, not eating at improper times, and live purely.

Third, one who upholds the pure precepts must not take part in worldly affairs, must not act as a messenger, must not practice spells, must not make elixirs, must not befriend the powerful and noble, and must not treat fellow practitioners with contempt; none of these should be done. One should rectify one's own mind and maintain right mindfulness so as to seek liberation.

Fourth, one who upholds the pure precepts must not conceal his own faults and errors, must not display supernormal powers to show off and confuse the people, and with respect to the four kinds of support (food, clothing, bedding, and medicine), should know the measure and be content, and should not store them up.

[Timely food] This refers to eating once at midday, that is, from after daybreak in the morning until before the sun reaches its height at noon, one may beg and eat food; this is called “timely food.” Eating after noon until before daybreak the next morning is called “untimely food.” [Intimate and rude] Treating fellow practitioners with contempt. “Intimate” refers to those with close relations. “Rude (
xiè

)”, also written “xiè màn,” means frivolous and contemptuous. [Four offerings] Food, clothing, bedding, and medicine. [Obtaining what is needed for support] Obtaining the objects of support. “Qù” is interchangeable with “qǔ” (to take). [A brief statement of the marks of upholding the precepts] Master Ouyi, in his Explanation, says: “The essence of the precepts is single, what is called the non-created; the marks of the precepts are extremely many, what are called the five divisions and seven categories. Here I cite those that ordinary feelings most easily violate, hence it is called a ‘brief statement.’”

[Five divisions and seven categories] The bhikṣu precepts and the bhikṣuṇī precepts are usually divided into five divisions and seven categories, that is, seven categories of offenses in five grades. [Three karma] Karma of body, karma of speech, and karma of mind. The karma of body is what the body does, such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and drunkenness; the karma of speech is what the mouth utters, such as harsh speech, divisive speech, idle talk, and false speech; the karma of mind is what the mind thinks, such as the arising of greed, anger, and delusion.

[The precepts are the root of correct and conformable liberation, hence they are called the Prātimokṣa. By relying on these precepts, one gains the various concentrations and the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.]

The precepts are the root of correct and conformable liberation, hence they are called liberation in every place (the Prātimokṣa). Because by relying on these pure precepts, one gains concentration and the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.

Therefore, if a practitioner wishes to be correctly and conformably liberated, he must take these precepts as the root. From precepts concentration arises, from concentration wisdom is produced; concentration and wisdom both arise from the precepts.
[Gain the various concentrations] To produce concentration. Here “various” is a particle with no real meaning.

blocks.text: 5. The Merit of Upholding the Precepts

inline.s: [Therefore, bhikṣus, you should uphold the pure precepts and must not let them be destroyed or defective. If a person can uphold the pure precepts, then he can have wholesome dharmas; if there are no pure precepts, then no meritorious virtues can arise. Hence you should know that the precepts are the first dwelling place of secure merit.]

For this reason, bhikṣus should uphold the pure precepts and must not destroy or violate them. If a person can uphold the pure precepts, then he can possess all wholesome dharmas; if there are no pure precepts, then no meritorious virtue of goodness can arise. Therefore you should know that the precepts are the first dwelling place of secure (the “yin” is the same as “wen”, secure) merit.

Master Ouyi, in his Explanation, says: “In this there are altogether five exhortations: First, ‘should uphold the pure precepts’ admonishes not to lose one's own essence. Second, ‘must not let them be destroyed or defective’ admonishes not to abandon the means. Third, ‘can have wholesome dharmas’ admonishes to constantly accumulate merit. Fourth, ‘if there are no pure precepts,’ etc., admonishes to know the many evils. Fifth, ‘the dwelling place of secure merit’ admonishes to abide in the place of security and not dwell in a place of insecurity.”

[You bhikṣus, having already been able to abide in the precepts, should control the five faculties and not let them run loose and enter the five desires. It is like a cowherd who, holding his staff, watches over the cattle and does not let them roam and damage others’ crops. If one lets go the five faculties, not only will the five desires have no limit and be uncontrollable, but it is also like an unruly horse that, not held by the bridle, will drag a person into a pit. Being robbed by thieves is suffering for only this life; the calamity of the five faculties as thieves brings disaster for many lives. The harm is very great - you must be careful! Therefore the wise control them and do not follow them, guarding them as if they were thieves, and never letting them run loose; even if one were to let them go, one would soon see them worn away.]

You bhikṣus, having already been able to abide in the precepts, should control and discipline the five faculties and not let them run loose and enter the five desires. It is like a cowherd who, holding his staff in hand, watches over the cattle and does not let them run off and eat others’ crops. If one lets go the five faculties, not only will the five desires blaze without limit and be uncontrollable, but it is also like riding an unruly horse that, not guided by the reins, will certainly harm a person and make him fall into a deep pit. Being robbed and harmed by thieves is suffering for only this life; but if one suffers the calamity of the five faculties as thieves, one will suffer disaster for many lives. The harm of the five faculties is very great - you must be careful! Therefore the wise always tightly control their own five faculties without the least slackening, guarding them as if defending against thieves, and never giving them an opening to act; even if for a moment through negligence the five faculties enter the five desires, one should promptly pull them back.

After the Buddha taught how to abide in the precepts and the merit of abiding in them, he immediately turned to the key to guarding the precepts: “Control the five faculties and do not let them run loose and enter the five desires.”

[Five faculties] The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body. [Five desires] The desire for forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and tangibles. Form means beautiful appearances; sound means pleasing sounds and charming words; scent means fragrant odors; taste means delicious flavors; and tangible means agreeable touch. Because these five can cause people to give rise to thoughts of greed, they are called the five desires. Upholding the precepts purely means being able to control the five faculties and not be moved by the five desires.

Yanzi's four “do nots” (do not look at what is contrary to propriety, do not listen to what is contrary to propriety, do not speak what is contrary to propriety, do not act contrary to propriety) likewise strictly control the five faculties so as not to enter the five desires. “Propriety” is a standard of conduct: the Confucians have their standard of conduct, and the standard of conduct of the Buddha's children is the Prātimokṣa (the precepts).

[Yanzi] Yan Hui, a student of Confucius. He was good at the effort of overcoming himself, strictly keeping to not looking at what is contrary to propriety, not listening to what is contrary to propriety, not speaking what is contrary to propriety, and not acting contrary to propriety.

blocks.text: 7. Bring the Mind Under Single Control

inline.s: [These five faculties have the mind as their lord; therefore you should carefully control the mind. The mind is more to be feared than a poisonous snake, a fierce beast, or a resentful robber; even a great fire leaping overstepping is not enough as a metaphor. It is like someone who, holding a vessel of honey, moves about lightly and restlessly, seeing only the honey and not the deep pit. It is like a mad elephant without a hook, or a monkey that has gained a tree, leaping and jumping, hard to restrain. You should quickly crush it and not let it run loose. One who lets go this mind loses the good works of a person; one who controls it in a single place succeeds in everything. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should diligently and earnestly subdue your mind.]

These five faculties (the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body) have the mind as their lord; therefore you must take good care to control your own mind. A scattered mind is more to be feared than a poisonous snake, a fierce beast, or a resentful robber - even a sky-filling fire is not as fearsome. It is like someone who holds up a bowl of honey, smugly self-satisfied, seeing only the honey in the bowl and not the deep pit before him. Again it is like a mad elephant with no iron hook to control it, galloping far and wide; and like a monkey that has run into a forest, leaping and jumping, hard to restrain. With the slightest scattering of the mind, one should immediately subdue it (pull it back) and not let it run loose. One who lets go this mind loses the good works of a person; one who controls the mind in a single place succeeds in everything. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should diligently and earnestly tame your minds.
This is to say: the mind is the lord of the five faculties and directs them, so if one wishes to control the five faculties, one must first control the mind.

[Carefully control the mind] To work hard at controlling the mind. [Mad elephant without a hook] The “mad elephant” is a metaphor for the mind's mad delusion, and “without a hook” is a metaphor for losing control. The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: “The mind is light, restless, and ever-turning, hard to grasp and hard to tune; it gallops and runs away, like a great evil elephant.” It also says: “It is like a mad drunken elephant, foolish and violent, greatly given to killing. There is an elephant-tamer who, with a great iron hook, hooks it on the top of its head, and it is immediately tamed, and its malicious mind is entirely gone. All sentient beings are likewise.” [Stupid (
ái

)] Foolish. [Good works] The wholesome dharmas of humans and gods and the supramundane wholesome dharmas are collectively called good works. [Subdue your mind] This says: the mind is a servant; it must not be indulged, much less allowed to be the master. Rather one should oneself take charge of the mind and steer it. Therefore practice is the cultivation of the mind - taming the mind is the practice of the cowherd.

[You bhikṣus, when you receive various foods and drink, you should be like taking medicine, and with respect to good or bad, you should not give rise to increase or decrease [of preference]. Only seek to support the body, so as to remove hunger and thirst. Just as a bee gathers flowers, only taking their taste and not harming their color or fragrance; so too a bhikṣu, receiving others’ offerings, only seeks to remove his own afflictions, should not seek much, lest it destroy his good heart. It is like the wise person who measures how much a cow's strength can bear, and does not let it be overloaded so as to exhaust its strength.]

You bhikṣus, when you receive offerings of food and drink, you should be like taking medicine, which is only to sustain the body; therefore you must not seek the good and resent the bad. Obtaining food and drink is to support the body and remove hunger and thirst. When receiving offerings, you should be like a bee gathering flowers, only taking their taste and not harming their color or fragrance; so too a bhikṣu, receiving others’ offerings, while obtaining what he needs, should also avoid causing the donor affliction, and should not seek much and thereby injure the donor's good heart. This is like the wise person who, according to the cow's strength, determines its burden, and does not let it be overworked.

[Receive various foods and drink, be like taking medicine] Medicine is to cure illness and food is to cure hunger; as long as hunger is cured, that is enough, and one should not greedily seek color, scent, or taste. [Only seek to sustain the body] To take in order to support the body. “Qù” is interchangeable with “qǔ” (to take); “zhī” (branch) means support.

[You bhikṣus, by day you should diligently cultivate the mind in wholesome dharmas, and do not let the time pass in vain; in the early night and the late night, too, you must not be idle. In the middle of the night recite the scriptures and so refresh yourself. Do not, on account of sleep, let a whole life pass in vain, with nothing gained. You should think on the fire of impermanence, which burns all the world, and seek early to save yourself; do not sleep! The various afflictions, as thieves, are always lying in wait to kill people, more so than a resentful enemy; how can you sleep and not be vigilant and awake? The affliction, like a poisonous snake, sleeps in your heart, just as a black viper sleeps in your chamber; you should use the hook of the precepts to expel it early. Once the sleeping snake is out, then you may sleep peacefully; if it is not out and you sleep, you are a shameless person! The garment of shame and conscience is the foremost of all adornments. Conscience is like an iron hook that can restrain a person from what is unlawful; therefore you should always have shame and conscience, never for a moment setting it aside. If you depart from shame and conscience, you lose all meritorious virtues. A person of conscience has wholesome dharmas; one without conscience is no different from the various animals.]

You bhikṣus, by day you should diligently cultivate the mind in wholesome dharmas and not let the time pass in vain; in the early night and the late night you must not be idle either. In the middle of the night you should silently recite the scriptures and then sleep, so as to maintain right mindfulness without losing it. Do not, on account of dullness and sleep, let a whole life pass in vain, with nothing gained. You should think on the blazing fire of impermanence (that is, death), which is even now burning this world, and must seek early to save yourself in order to escape birth and death; do not be attached to sleep! The various afflictions, as thieves, are always lurking, scheming to kill people; they are more sinister and cruel than your resentful enemy - how can you sleep deeply and not be vigilant? Affliction, in your mind, is like a poisonous snake sleeping in your chamber; you must use the iron hook of the precepts to remove it as quickly as possible. Once the sleeping snake of affliction is removed, you may sleep peacefully; if it is not removed and you sleep, you are a shameless person! To know shame is the most adorned garment, able to ward off the invasion of all kinds of temptations. Shame is also like an iron hook that can subdue a heart like a mad elephant so as not to do unlawful things. Therefore at all times and in all places you should maintain shame and never lose it, even for a moment. If you depart from shame, you lose all meritorious virtues. A person of shame has wholesome dharmas; one without shame is no different from the animals.

[Wholesome dharmas] Dharmas that accord with principle and benefit people. Such as the five precepts and the ten good deeds, which are the wholesome dharmas of the world, and the three studies and the six perfections, which are the supramundane wholesome dharmas. [Three studies] The study of precepts, the study of concentration, and the study of wisdom. “Precepts” are the prohibitions, what the Vinaya Pitaka elucidates, which can prevent people from creating all evil karma of body, speech, and mind; “concentration” is meditative absorption, what the Sutra Pitaka elucidates, which enables people to still their thoughts and clarify the mind; “wisdom” is prajñā, what the Commentarial Pitaka elucidates, which enables people to comprehend the truth and cut off ignorance. By cultivating these three studies, one gains concentration from the precepts, wisdom from concentration, and ultimately attains the fruit of the undefiled path; hence the three studies are also called the “three undefiled studies.” [Undefiled] “Defilement” is another name for affliction; to be undefiled is to have no affliction. [Six perfections] Also called the six pāramitās, the six practices by which one can cross from this shore of birth-and-death and suffering to the other shore of nirvāṇa's bliss: giving, precepts, patience, diligence, concentration, and prajñā. Giving crosses over stinginess and greed; precepts cross over transgression; patience crosses over anger; diligence crosses over idleness; concentration crosses over scattering; and prajñā crosses over ignorance. [Viper (yuán)] A kind of poisonous snake spoken of in old books.

blocks.text: 10. Do Not Give Rise to Anger

inline.s: [You bhikṣus, if someone comes to cut you limb from limb, you should gather your own mind and not give rise to anger; you should also guard your mouth and not utter evil words. If you let go the mind of hatred, you hinder your own path and lose the benefit of merit. The virtue of patience cannot be equaled by upholding the precepts or ascetic practice. One who can practice patience may be called a great man of strength. If one cannot joyfully endure the poison of evil abuse as if drinking sweet dew, one cannot be called a wise one who has entered the path. Why? The harm of anger destroys all wholesome dharmas and ruins a good reputation. In this life and the next, people do not delight to see him. You should know that the mind of anger is more fierce than a raging fire, and you should always guard against it and never let it enter. Among the thieves that rob merit, none exceeds anger. The white-robed layman, caught up in the five desires, is not a cultivator of the path and cannot control himself, so his anger may be forgiven; but a renunciant cultivating the path, a person without desire, who yet harbors anger - this is inadmissible indeed. It is like lightning kindling a fire in the clear and cool clouds - that is not what should be.]

You bhikṣus, if someone comes to cut you limb from limb, you should gather your own mind and not give rise to hatred; you should also guard your mouth and not utter evil words. If you let go the mind of hatred, you hinder your own career of the path and lose merit. The virtue of patience cannot be equaled by upholding the precepts or ascetic practice. One who can practice patience may be called a great man of strength. If one cannot joyfully endure the poison of evil abuse as if drinking sweet dew, one cannot be called a wise one who has entered the path. Why? The harm of anger is very great - it can destroy all wholesome dharmas and ruin a good reputation. In this life and even in the next, everyone loathes you. You should know that the mind of anger is more fearsome than a raging fire, and you should always guard against it, never letting it arise. Among the thieves that plunder merit, none is more fierce than anger. The layman (white-robed), being in the midst of the five desires, and not a cultivator of the path, cannot control himself, so his anger may be forgiven; but a renunciant cultivating the path, who has already left desire yet harbors anger - this is absolutely inadmissible. It is like lightning and fire bursting forth in the clear, quiet white clouds - this is indeed most improper!

[Cut limb from limb] To cut the body into pieces. In the Diamond Sutra, the Buddha said: in the past, when practicing on the causal ground, he was cut limb from limb by King Kali, yet did not give rise to anger. [Causal ground] From the stage of an ordinary being first giving rise to the mind of seeking Buddhahood, up to before the fulfillment of Buddhahood, this whole process is called the “causal ground.” [Entering the path] To abandon worldly dharmas and enter the Buddha path; in other words, to leave home. [Sweet dew] Sweet nectar. The Annotated Vimalakīrti Sutra says: “The gods place all kinds of precious medicines in the sea, and with a mountain of jewels grind them so that they become sweet dew. Eating it, one attains immortality; it is called the deathless medicine.”

Master Ouyi said: “Upholding the precepts with a self-centered mind, the reward is only in the realm of humans and gods; practicing patience with non-self, one achieves the supramundane great path. To be wronged yet not contend (not to calculate), is like the vast sea and open sky, allowing the kite to fly and the fish to leap - hence it is called ‘a great man of strength.’”

[You bhikṣus, you should rub your own head, having already abandoned ornaments and finery, wearing the bad-colored robe, holding the response-vessel, and living by begging. Seeing yourself thus, if arrogance arises, you should swiftly destroy it. To grow in arrogance is not even fitting for the worldly white-robed layman, much less for one who has left home to enter the path, who for the sake of liberation humbles himself and goes begging?]

You bhikṣus, you should often rub your head to remind yourselves: I, for the sake of seeking the path, have abandoned the world's wealth, fame, and position, contenting myself to be beneath others, wearing the bad-colored robe, holding a bowl and begging food to live. How then can I give rise again to arrogance and obstruct the path? Having this realization and insight, once arrogance arises, you should immediately destroy it. To grow in one's arrogance is not even fitting for the worldly layman (white-robed), much less for oneself, a renunciant cultivator of the path, who for the sake of liberation has voluntarily lowered his station and goes begging?

[Bad-colored robe] The monk's robe. The Collection of Translated Terms says: “In Sanskrit it is called kasāya; here it is called the bad-colored robe, meaning it is not one of the five proper colors.” [Response-vessel] Also called the response-measure vessel, that is, the iron bowl used by a bhikṣu when begging food.
A verse says: One bowl, the meals of a thousand homes; a lone monk, roaming ten thousand miles; for the sake of the matter of birth and death, begging his way through spring and autumn.

[For the sake of the matter of birth and death, begging his way through spring and autumn] To settle the great matter of birth and death, begging food to carry on, as spring goes and autumn comes, year after year.

[You bhikṣus, a fawning and crooked mind is contrary to the Way. Therefore you should make your mind upright and straightforward. You should know that fawning and crookedness are only deceit; for one who has entered the path, there is no place for such things. Therefore you should rectify your minds and take uprightness as the root.]

O monks, a mind of flattery and sycophancy (bending to please others) runs contrary to the Way. Therefore, you should make your mind upright. Know that flattery and sycophancy serve only to deceive oneself and others; for one who cultivates the Way this is absolutely impermissible. Therefore you should correct your mind and take straightforwardness as its foundation.

[Straightforwardness] Zhi means upright; 'straightforwardness' is rectitude. An upright mind has no flattery or sycophancy. The Buddha Way lies in awakening to the innate naturalness originally possessed by all beings; this mind is the root of all practices. [Correcting the mind] To correct and solemnize one's own mind.

Master Ouyi said: 'Words that flatter and seek to please are called sycophancy; thoughts that bend and waver with circumstances are called crookedness. Sycophancy is not straightforwardness, and crookedness is not uprightness. One only deceives oneself and also deceives others; such a person is by no means one who has entered the Way. An upright mind is the place of practice; because the heart's words are straight, it never has any crooked appearance. If one lacks right mindfulness of true reality, how can one be called "correcting the mind"?'

[O monks, know that a person of many desires seeks gain lavishly and therefore has much suffering and distress; a person of few desires seeks nothing and wants nothing, and so is free of this affliction. Even the simple state of few desires is worth cultivating, how much more so when few desires can give rise to all manner of merit! A person of few desires does not flatter and bend to win others' approval, nor is he drawn along by his faculties. One who practices few desires is calm and open, with no anxiety or fear. Whatever he encounters, he has abundance and is never in want. One who has few desires attains Nirvana. This is called having few desires!]

O monks, you should know that a person of many desires, because he seeks gain lavishly, has much suffering and distress; a person of few desires seeks nothing and wants nothing, so he is free of this affliction. Since even the simple state of few desires is free of this affliction, one should already cultivate few desires; how much more so when few desires can give rise to all manner of merit and accomplish countless holy and wholesome dharmas! A person of few desires does not flatter and bend to please others, nor is he dragged along by the five faculties into attachment to the five desires. One who practices few desires contends with no one, seeks nothing in the world, and so his mind is broad and open, at ease and natural, with no worry or fear. In whatever circumstances he always has abundance and never feels want. One who is able to have few desires can realize Nirvana. This is why one should have few desires!

[O monks, if you wish to free yourselves from all suffering and distress, you should contemplate contentment. The practice of contentment is the abode of wealth, happiness, and peace. A contented person, though he lies upon the ground, is still at ease and joyful; one who is discontent, though he dwells in heaven, is still not satisfied. The discontented, though rich, are poor; the contented, though poor, are rich. The discontented are ever dragged by the five desires and are pitied by the contented. This is called contentment!]

O monks, if you wish to free yourselves from the many kinds of suffering and distress, you should contemplate contentment. The practice of contentment is the abode of wealth, happiness, and peace. A contented person, though he sleeps on the ground, still feels joy and peace; one who is discontent, though in heaven, is never satisfied. The discontented, though wealthy, always feel want; the contented, though poor, always feel rich. The discontented are ever dragged by the five desires to create karma and receive retribution, and are pitied and sighed over by the contented. This is why one should be contented!
[An-yin (secure)] It means stable and secure. Here 'yin' is the same as 'wen' (stable).
To have few desires is to seek nothing outwardly; to be contented is to be inwardly fulfilled.

[O monks, if you seek stillness and the peace of non-doing, you should depart from turmoil and dwell alone in quiet. The person of quiet places is honored and respected by Shakra and all the gods. Therefore, you should give up your own followers and the followers of others, and in solitude contemplate how to extinguish the root of suffering. One who delights in crowds receives the afflictions of the crowd; for example, a great tree on which many birds gather is in danger of withering and breaking. Those bound in the world sink into the mass of suffering, like an old elephant trapped in mud, unable to free itself. This is called dwelling far from turmoil!]

O monks, if you seek stillness and have the peace of non-doing, you should depart from noise and dwell alone. The person of quiet solitude is honored by Shakra and all the gods. Therefore, you should leave your own followers and the followers of others, and in solitude contemplate the root of extinguishing suffering. One who delights in being among people contracts the afflictions of people; for example, a great tree on which many birds nest is liable to wither and break. In this way one is bound by the world and sinks into the mass of suffering, like an aged elephant trapped in a swamp, unable to struggle free. This is why one should stay far from turmoil!

[Kui-nao (turmoil)] Uproar and clamor. [Xian-ju (dwelling in quiet)] Dwelling alone in one place. [Di-shi (Shakra)] The lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven. [Di-shi zhu tian (Shakra and the gods)] Shakra and the heavenly gods. [One's own group and others] 'One's own group' means one's own teacher, students, and companions; 'others' means the circle of outsiders. [Contemplating the extinction of the root of suffering] To contemplate uprooting suffering at its very root, far from its cause. [An old elephant sunk in mud] Like an aged elephant sinking in a swamp; the 'old elephant' is a metaphor for one worn out by the tangle of external conditions.
The Ten Virtues of Dwelling in Quiet
1. No encounters between men and women, no heart of lust; 2. No occasion for idle talk, no fault of false speech;
3. No enemies to face, no fear of quarrels; 4. No friends of right and wrong, no error of praise and blame;
5. No seeing others' failures, no speaking of others' faults; 6. No trailing after kinsfolk, no attachment to family;
7. No persons face to face, no vexation of etiquette; 8. No arriving guests, no feasting and entertaining to manage;
9. No dealing with crowds, no hope of fine clothes; 10. Alone in the practice of the wondrous way, free from all other hindrances.

[O monks, if you are diligent and vigorous, nothing is difficult for you. Therefore, you should be diligent and vigorous, for example, as a small stream that flows constantly can wear through stone. If the mind of a practitioner relaxes and falters again and again, it is like drilling for fire and resting before the wood is hot; though you want to obtain fire, fire is hard to obtain. This is called vigor!]

O monks, if you cultivate the Way diligently and vigorously, nothing can stand against you. Therefore, you should be diligent and vigorous, just as drops of water falling ceaselessly can drip through stone. If a practitioner's mind is often slothful and neglectful, this is like drilling wood for fire and resting before the wood becomes hot. Drilling and stopping, stopping and drilling, though you wish to draw out fire, the fire will not come. This is why one should be diligently relentless!
[Shuo-shuo (again and again)] Repeatedly; often.
That water drips through stone is entirely due to the merit of unceasing persistence.

[O monks, seeking a good spiritual friend, seeking good protection and aid, nothing is like not forgetting mindfulness. For one who does not forget mindfulness, the thieves of the afflictions cannot enter. Therefore, you should always hold mindfulness gathered in the mind. If mindfulness is lost, all merit is lost. If the power of mindfulness is firm and strong, though you enter among the thieves of the five desires, you are not harmed by them, just as one who dons armor and enters the battle line has no fear. This is called not forgetting mindfulness!]

O monks, seeking the instruction of a good spiritual friend and seeking the protection and aid of good devotees are both beneath not forgetting right mindfulness. For one who does not forget right mindfulness, the thieves of the afflictions cannot intrude. Therefore, you should always hold right mindfulness gathered in the mind. If right mindfulness is lost, all merit is lost. If the power of right mindfulness is firm and strong, though you enter among the thieves of the five desires, you are not harmed by them, just as one who wears armor and enters the enemy line has no fear. This is why one should not forget right mindfulness!

[Not forgetting mindfulness] Not forgetting right mindfulness. [Right mindfulness] The thought of the true Dharma, for example the Buddha-name of a reciter of the Buddha, the mantra of one who holds a mantra, or the huato of one who meditates in Chan. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says: 'If the mind runs scattered, then gather it back and dwell in right mindfulness.'
Not forgetting right mindfulness is the foremost of all practices.

[O monks, if you gather the mind, the mind becomes concentrated. Because the mind is in concentration, it can know the characteristics of arising and ceasing in the world. Therefore, you should always diligently cultivate the concentrations. One who attains concentration has a mind that does not scatter. For example, a household that treasures water well manages its dikes and ponds; a practitioner is likewise. For the sake of the water of wisdom, he cultivates meditation well, so that it is not lost. This is called concentration!]

O monks, if you can gather your scattered thoughts, then you can rest the mind on one object and attain concentration. Because the mind is in concentration, it can clearly discern the characteristics of arising and ceasing in the world. Therefore, you should always diligently cultivate the various concentrations. One who attains concentration has a mind that is not scattered. Just as a farm household that treasures water well manages its dikes and ponds, so too a practitioner, for the sake of treasuring the water of wisdom, cultivates meditation well, so that the water of wisdom is not lost. This is why one should gather the mind and enter concentration!

Master Ouyi said: 'When the mind is in concentration, it is like the bright sun hanging in the sky, clearly illuminating all things, and so it can know the characteristics of arising and ceasing in the world.'

[Concentration] Resting the mind on a single object without letting it scatter is called concentration. [Characteristics of arising and ceasing] The characteristics of the world are nothing else but the phenomena of arising and ceasing, ceasing and arising, this arising-and-ceasing and ceasing-and-arising without end; therefore they are called the characteristics of arising and ceasing.

[O monks, if you have wisdom, you have no clinging and attachment. Always examine yourself and do not let it be lost; thus, in my Dharma you can gain liberation. If it is not so, you are neither a cultivator of the Way nor a layperson, and you are nothing at all. A person of true wisdom is a sturdy ship for crossing the sea of old age, sickness, and death; he is a great bright lamp in the darkness of ignorance; he is the good medicine for all the sick; he is the sharp axe that fells the tree of the afflictions. Therefore, you should increase your own wisdom through the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection, and the wisdom of practice. If a person has the illumination of wisdom, though he has no divine eye, he is a clear-sighted person. This is called wisdom!]

O monks, if you have wisdom, you will not cling and be attached. Therefore, you must always examine yourself and not let wisdom be lost; this way, in my Buddha-Dharma you can gain liberation. If it is not so, you are neither a renunciate cultivating the Way nor a layperson studying Buddhism, and you are nothing at all. Full and solid wisdom is the sturdy treasure-ship for crossing the great sea of old age, sickness, and death; it is the great bright lamp in the darkness of ignorance; it is the good medicine for all the sick; it is the sharp axe that fells the tree of the afflictions. Therefore, you should increase your wisdom through hearing, reflection, and practice. If a person has the illumination of wisdom, though he has no divine eye, he is a clear-sighted person. This is why one should never lose wisdom!

[A person of true wisdom] 'Real wisdom' means full and solid wisdom. 'Zhe' (one who) here is a modal particle that marks a pause in tone and forms a sentence of judgment. For example: Chen Sheng, (he) was a man of Yangcheng. [Wisdom of hearing, wisdom of reflection, wisdom of practice] The wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection, and the wisdom of practice. The wisdom of hearing is the wisdom born from hearing the Dharma; the wisdom of reflection is the wisdom born from reflecting on Buddhist principles; the wisdom of practice is the wisdom born from diligent cultivation of meditation.

[O monks, through all kinds of idle talk the mind becomes disturbed; though one has left home, one has not yet gained release. Therefore, monks, you should quickly abandon the idle talk that disturbs the mind. If you wish to attain the joy of still extinction, you must well put an end to the affliction of idle talk. This is called not speaking idly!]

O monks, in speaking and hearing all kinds of idle talk, the mind becomes disturbed; though you have left home, in fact you have not yet freed yourselves from the bonds of the world. Therefore, you should immediately abandon the idle talk that disturbs the mind. If you wish to attain the joy of still extinction, you must well put an end to this calamity of idle talk. This is why one should not speak idly!
[Idle talk] Erroneous and meaningless speech. That is, speech that opposes truth, merely disturbs the mind and wastes time, and cannot increase wholesome dharmas.

[O monks, toward all these merits, you should always be single-minded, renouncing all negligence as you would flee a vengeful enemy. The benefits spoken by the great compassionate World-Honored One are all complete and ultimate; you should only diligently practice them. Whether in the mountains, in a desolate marsh, beneath a tree, or in a quiet chamber, be mindful of the Dharma you have received and do not let it be lost. Always encourage yourselves and practice diligently; do not die in vain and afterwards regret. I am like a good physician who knows the illness and prescribes the medicine; whether you take it or not is not the physician's fault. I am also like a good guide who leads people onto the good path; hearing it yet not practicing is not the fault of the guide.]

O monks, toward all the merits and dharmas spoken above, you should practice them with a single mind, renouncing all negligence as you would stay far from a vengeful enemy. I, the great compassionate World-Honored One, have spoken of the dharmas that benefit liberation, and they are all the path of ultimacy; you must diligently practice them. Whether in the mountains, in a desolate marsh, beneath a tree, or in a quiet chamber, hold to the Dharma you have received and do not let it be lost. Always encourage yourselves and practice diligently; do not waste your whole life in vain and then regret. I am like a good physician who knows your illness and tells you the remedy; whether you take it or not is beyond the physician's responsibility. I am also like an excellent guide who leads you along the golden road of liberation; but you do not follow, and this is not the fault of the guide.
[Negligence] Letting the mind run loose and acting willfully and wantonly.

blocks.text: 22. The Four Noble Truths Encompass All

inline.s: [If any of you have doubt about the four truths of suffering and the rest, you should ask at once; do not harbor doubt and fail to seek resolution. At that time the World-Honored One thus proclaimed three times, and no one asked. Why? Because the assembly had no doubt.]

If any of you still have doubt about the four truths of suffering, its origination, its cessation, and the path, you can ask at once. Do not harbor doubt and fail to seek an answer. At that time the World-Honored One thus loudly asked three times, yet no one asked. Why? Because everyone had no doubt.

[The four truths] These are the four noble truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. 'Di' (truth) means truth. First, the truth of suffering explains the truth that life is full of suffering. Suffering is characterized by oppression. Life has the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and countless sufferings; suffering is the truth of actual life. Second, the 'ji' of the truth of origination means bringing about or creating; it is the truth that explains the cause of suffering, that is, where the pain of life comes from. The suffering of life arises because craving produces karma, and so one suffers and transmigrates. Third, the truth of cessation explains the truth of extinguishing all suffering. When all the origination of suffering, that is, craving, is cut off forever without remainder, without defilement and without attachment, one no longer suffers or transmigrates; this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the truth of the path explains how to extinguish forever the origination of suffering, that is, craving, which is the path that ends suffering, the eightfold noble path. Among the four noble truths, origination is the cause and suffering is the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation is the fruit.

[The three sufferings] The suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned existence. The suffering of suffering: people already have a body of birth and death, which is suffering enough; on top of that the many sufferings press upon them, so that suffering is added to suffering; hence it is called the suffering of suffering. The suffering of change is the suffering felt when an occasionally appearing blissful state is lost. The suffering of conditioned existence is the suffering of all conditions being impermanent, flowing on without rest, and never settled. [The eight sufferings] First, the suffering of birth, the pain at birth; second, the suffering of old age, the pain of aging and weakness; third, the suffering of sickness, the pain of illness; fourth, the suffering of death, the pain at the moment of death; fifth, the suffering of separation from the loved, the pain of parting from what one loves; sixth, the suffering of meeting with the hated, the pain of encountering those one resents; seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the pain of wishes unfulfilled; eighth, the suffering of the blazing of the five aggregates, that is, the fierce burning activity of the five aggregates covering over true nature.

[The eightfold noble path] Also called the eightfold right path, the eight paths of the noble ones: first, right view, correct seeing and understanding; second, right intention, correct thinking; third, right speech, correct words; fourth, right action, correct conduct; fifth, right livelihood, correct occupation and way of life; sixth, right effort, correct striving; seventh, right mindfulness, correct awareness; eighth, right concentration, correct meditation. Cultivating this eightfold noble path, one can realize the fruit of Arhatship.

[Then Aniruddha, observing the minds of the assembly, said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! The moon can be made hot, and the sun can be made cold, but the four truths spoken by the Buddha cannot be changed. The Buddha says the truth of suffering is truly suffering and cannot be made pleasure; origination is truly the cause, with no other cause; if suffering is extinguished, then the cause is extinguished, and because the cause is extinguished the fruit is extinguished; the path that extinguishes suffering is truly the true path, with no other path. World-Honored One! These monks are certain and without doubt regarding the four truths.]

Then Aniruddha, observing the minds of the assembly, reported to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Even if the moon can be made hot and the sun can be made cold, the four truths spoken by the Buddha cannot be altered. The Buddha speaks of 'suffering': this is real suffering and cannot be turned into pleasure; 'origination' is the real cause of suffering, with no other cause; to extinguish suffering one must extinguish this cause of origination; the 'path' that extinguishes this cause of origination is truly the true path, with no other path. World-Honored One! We monks are now certain and without any doubt about the four truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path.
[Aniruddha] That is Aniruddha, one of the Buddha's ten great disciples, renowned as foremost in the divine eye.

[Among this assembly, those whose task is not yet accomplished, seeing the Buddha's passing, will certainly grieve. Those newly entered into the Dharma, hearing what the Buddha has said, will all be saved; for example, seeing lightning in the night, they immediately see the Way. Those whose task is accomplished and have crossed the sea of suffering only have this thought: how swift indeed is the World-Honored One's passing!]

Aniruddha continued: Among the assembly present, those who have not yet severed the afflictions, seeing the Buddha's passing, will certainly feel sorrow and grief. Those newly entered into the Dharma, hearing what the Buddha has said above, will all be saved, for having heard this instruction, it is as if a flash of lightning appeared in the dark night, and they clearly see the path of liberation. Those arhats whose task is accomplished have already crossed the sea of suffering and no longer transmigrate; they only think: how swift indeed is the World-Honored One's passing!

[Task not yet accomplished] This refers to those of the first, second, and third fruits, whose afflictions are not yet wholly cut off. [Task accomplished] The arhat's afflictions are wholly cut off and he has escaped birth and death; therefore it is said his task is accomplished.

Aniruddha spoke of the three types of people in the assembly: first, those whose task is not yet accomplished, whose delusions of thought are not yet wholly cut off, and who therefore feel grief; second, those newly entered into the Dharma, who, hearing what the Buddha has said above, have clearly seen the path of liberation and will all be saved; third, the arhats whose task is accomplished, whose delusions of view and thought are wholly cut off, so they no longer have grief of affection, and they think: how swift indeed is the World-Honored One's passing!

[Although Aniruddha said these words, the whole assembly fully understood the meaning of the four noble truths. The World-Honored One, wishing to make this great assembly all firm and steadfast, in his great compassion again spoke to them: O monks, do not harbor grief and affliction. Even if I dwelt in the world for an eon, in the end I would also pass away; meeting without parting can never be obtained. The dharmas for benefiting oneself and benefiting others are all complete; if I remained long, there would be no further benefit. Those who can be saved, whether in heaven or among men, have all been saved; for those not yet saved, the causes and conditions for their salvation have already been established. From now on, my disciples practicing it in turn, this is how the Tathagata's Dharma body remains present and does not pass away.]

Although Aniruddha said these words, the assembly present fully understood the meaning of the four noble truths. The World-Honored One, wishing to enable them all to gain a firm and steadfast mind for the Way, in his great compassion again instructed the assembly: O monks, do not grieve and be afflicted. Even if I dwelt in the world for an eon, in the end I would enter into cessation; to meet and never part is impossible. The dharmas for benefiting oneself and benefiting others you already possess, and you can practice the Way relying on them. If I remained longer, there would be no further benefit. Those who can be saved, whether in heaven or among men, I have already saved; for those not yet saved, I have already planted the causes and conditions for their salvation. From now on, my disciples practicing the Way in turn, saving themselves and saving others, this is how the Tathagata's Dharma body remains present and does not pass away.

blocks.text: 25. All Things in the World Are Impermanent

inline.s: [Therefore, know that all things in the world are impermanent; meeting must be followed by parting. Do not harbor grief and affliction; such is the nature of the world. Be diligent and vigorous, and seek liberation early; with the light of wisdom, extinguish all the darkness of delusion. The world is truly perilous and fragile, with nothing firm and lasting. I now gain cessation, as one removes a dire illness. This is the body to be relinquished, a thing of sin and evil, falsely called a body, sunk in the great sea of old age, sickness, birth, and death. What wise person, being able to destroy it, would not rejoice as one who kills a vengeful enemy!]

Therefore, know that everything in the world is impermanent; where there is gathering there must be scattering. Do not harbor grief and affliction; such are all the phenomena of the world. Therefore, you should be diligent and vigorous, seeking liberation as early as possible, and with the light of wisdom extinguish all the darkness of ignorance and delusion. The world is truly perilous and fragile, with nothing firm and lasting. Today I enter cessation, as one removes a dire illness. This physical body is a body to be relinquished; it is a thing of sin and evil, falsely called a body, sunk in the great sea of old age, sickness, birth, and death. What wise person, being able to destroy this body, would not rejoice, as one who kills a vengeful enemy!

[O monks, always be single-minded and diligently seek the path that leads out of the world. All dharmas of the world, moving and unmoving, are all marks of decay and unrest. You should now stop; say no more. The time is about to pass; I wish to enter cessation. This is my final instruction.]

O monks, always be single-minded and diligently seek the noble path that leads out of birth and death. All dharmas of the world, moving and unmoving, are marks of decay and unrest. You should stop speaking; say no more. The time of the middle of the night is nearly past; I must enter Nirvana. These are my final instructions.

[Moving and unmoving dharmas] The desire realm is the moving dharma; the form realm and the formless realm are the unmoving dharmas. Though there is this distinction of moving and still, they all belong to impermanence and non-self, so one cannot but think of escaping them. [The three realms] The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world where beings with the two desires of sex and food dwell; from the six desire heavens above, through the four great continents where humans and animals live, down to the Uninterrupted Hell, all belong to it. The form realm is the world where beings free of the two desires of sex and food but still having form dwell; the eighteen heavens of the four dhyanas belong to it. The formless realm is the world where beings with neither form dwell, abiding their minds and consciousness in profound meditation; the four heavens of the immaterial sphere belong to it. These three realms are the spheres through which ordinary beings transmigrate in birth and death; therefore Buddhist practitioners take leaping out of the three realms as their aim.

Master Ouyi said: 'This final instruction is precisely the display of the testamentary teaching, the most excellent and most essential of all the dharmas that maintain the Dharma. Alas! This last earnest counsel is the utmost compassion! As a disciple, how should one not carve it into the marrow of one's bones and engrave it upon the liver!'
